Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current methods for 6D object pose estimation face a binary dilemma. "Instance-level" methods require precise, pre-scanned 3D CAD models, making them unusable for novel objects encountered in the wild. Conversely, "Model-free" methods attempt to estimate pose from reference images, but they typically require multi-view coverage (video) to understand the 3D structure.

A critical gap exists when we only have a **single RGB-D anchor image** of a novel object. In scenarios where the target view is drastically different from the anchor view (non-overlapping viewpoints) or heavily occluded, traditional feature matching fails because there are no shared visual features. Furthermore, while recent generative AI can "hallucinate" 3D shapes from single images, these generated shapes lack **metric scale** and alignment with the real world, rendering them useless for precise robotic manipulation tasks that require absolute spatial understanding.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can solve the "single-view novel object" problem by converting it from a partial-matching task into a pseudo-model-based task.

Our core intuition is that while generative "Image-to-3D" models lose metric scale, the single RGB-D anchor image contains sufficient geometric cues to recover it. We propose that by **jointly optimizing for object size and 6D pose**, we can align a normalized generative mesh to the partial depth observation of the anchor. Once this "hallucinated" mesh is rigid-locked to the real-world scale and anchor pose, it can serve as a complete 3D reference, enabling robust pose estimation in novel scenes even when the views are non-overlapping or occluded.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a three-stage pipeline designed to bridge the gap between normalized generative shapes and metric-scale robotic requirements.

**1. Normalized Shape Hallucination**
We will leverage off-the-shelf Image-to-3D generative models to predict a complete 3D mesh from the single RGB-D anchor crop. At this stage, the output will be in a normalized canonical space (unit scale) and unaligned with the camera coordinate system. This transforms our problem from "estimating pose from a 2D image" to "aligning a 3D shape to a depth map."

**2. Coarse-to-Fine Anchor Alignment (Metric Recovery)**
To recover the missing metric scale and align the shape to the anchor image:
*   **Coarse Alignment via Oriented Bounding Boxes:** We will compute an Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) for the visible point cloud in the anchor image to estimate the object's center and principal axes. This is more robust to partial visibility than simple coordinate averaging. We will roughly align the normalized mesh to this OBB to get an initial scale and rotation.
*   **Joint Size-Pose Refinement:** We will design a "Render-and-Compare" optimization loop. Unlike standard pose estimation which searches only for rotation and translation, our search space will expand to include **physical scale**. We will generate hypotheses with varying sizes and poses, render them, and compare them against the anchor observation. The hypothesis that maximizes alignment (e.g., volumetric overlap with the depth map) will define the object's true metric size and anchor pose.

**3. Query Pose Estimation (Full-to-Partial Matching)**
With the mesh now scaled and aligned to the anchor, we possess a "pseudo-ground-truth" CAD model. To find the relative pose of the object in a new target (query) scene:
*   We will treat the aligned mesh as a standard model.
*   We will apply a render-and-compare strategy to estimate the pose of this mesh within the query image.
*   The final relative transformation is derived by composing the transformation from the object to the anchor and from the object to the query.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Robustness to Non-Overlapping Views:** By reconstructing the full 3D shape, our method will enable pose estimation even when the anchor and query images show opposite sides of an object (zero visual overlap), a scenario where feature-matching methods fail.
*   **Single-View Metric Recovery:** We expect to demonstrate a reliable mechanism for recovering metric scale from a single RGB-D image by grounding generative 3D models in observed depth data.
*   **Model-Free Generalization:** This approach will allow robotic systems to manipulate completely novel objects without pre-existing CAD models or video scans, significantly increasing autonomy in unstructured environments.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

*   **Task:** Model-free 6D object pose estimation (determining relative rotation and translation) and size estimation of novel objects in novel scenes using a single RGB-D anchor image.
*   **Datasets:**
    *   **HO3D (V3):** Human-hand-object interactions. Evaluated on 4 objects across 13 video sequences (2,000 images). Large viewpoint variations and hand occlusions.
    *   **YCBInEOTA:** Dual-arm robot manipulations. Evaluated on 5 objects across 9 videos (749 frames). Diverse viewpoints and robot arm occlusions. Pairs sampled from DexYCB.
    *   **Toyota-Light:** Single-object pose estimation under challenging/varying lighting conditions. 2,000 image pairs.
    *   **REAL275:** Six object categories (3 instances per category) in different scenes. Limited viewpoint variations, minor occlusions. 2,000 image pairs.
    *   **LM-O (Linemod Occlusion):** Cluttered scenes with 12 distinct textureless objects.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **ADD:** Average Distance of Model Points (mean distance between corresponding 3D model points under predicted and GT poses). Used for asymmetric objects.
    *   **ADD-S:** Symmetric ADD (average distance to the closest model point). Used for symmetric objects.
    *   **AUC:** Area Under the Curve of ADD/ADD-S.
    *   **AR:** Average Recall (at threshold 0.1 times object diameter).
    *   **BOP Metrics:** Average Recall of Visual Surface Discrepancy (VSD), Maximum Symmetry-aware Surface Distance (MSSD), and Maximum Symmetry-aware Projection Distance (MSPD).
    *   **Chamfer Distance (CD):** For mesh quality evaluation.
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Oryon:** Multi-modal (RGB-D & Language) object pose estimation.
    *   **LoFTR:** Single-image matching baseline (RGB-D), combined with pose optimization.
    *   **Gedi:** Depth-based single-image matching baseline.
    *   **ObjectMatch:** Uses SuperGlue for match estimation.
    *   **SIFT:** Traditional feature matching baseline.
    *   **GigaPose:** RGB-based method (requires initial pose for size determination).
    *   **NeRF Baseline:** Object-centric NeRF trained on reference RGB-D image + Marching Cubes (used for shape ablation).
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Image-to-3D Model:** InstantMesh used for primary reconstruction (except where noted in LM-O experiments).
    *   **Size Sampling:** Size samples drawn in range $\Delta s \in [0.6, 1.4]$ along each axis (empirically set).
    *   **Refinement:** Used pose generation, refinement, and selection modules inspired by FoundationPose.
    *   **Segmentation:** Ground-truth segmentation masks used for HO3D, YCBInEOTA, Toyota-Light, and REAL275. CNOS used for LM-O.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Method Performance & Comparison:**
*   **Occlusions and Non-overlapping Views:**
    *   We observed that competing methods (Oryon, LoFTR, Gedi) struggled in scenarios where the anchor and query images had no overlapping parts or significant occlusions.
    *   Oryon and LoFTR failed to handle limited visibility of key features in the anchor image.
    *   Gedi (depth-based) exhibited ambiguity when dealing with RGB-based non-symmetric objects.
    *   Our method effectively reconstructed complete object shapes, allowing for robust pose estimation even when parts of the object were occluded or not visible in the anchor view.
*   **Specific Case Studies (HO3D & YCBInEOTA):**
    *   *White Cleanser:* When only a portion was visible in the anchor and the viewpoint changed significantly in the query, our method estimated the pose accurately, while baselines failed.
    *   *SPAM Can:* In cases where the anchor showed the back view and the query showed the logo side (partially occluded), our method successfully estimated the correct pose. Baselines failed due to reliance on limited anchor information.
    *   *Blue Pitcher:* Gedi roughly estimated the center position but failed the orientation. Our method successfully aligned both rotational and translational components.
    *   *Red Cracker Box:* Our method accurately aligned position and orientation even when the anchor showed the front cheese logo and the query showed the back view.
    *   *Mustard Bottle:* Our method maintained accurate pose estimation during interactions involving dual robot arms, demonstrating robustness to gripper occlusions.
*   **Lighting Sensitivity (Toyota-Light):**
    *   Our method showed robustness under varying lighting conditions, consistently outperforming Oryon.
*   **Generalization (REAL275):**
    *   Our method excelled in ADD(-S), AR, MSSD, and MSPD, indicating superior generalization across object categories compared to Oryon, though VSD performance was comparable.

**Ablation & Component Analysis:**
*   **Center Estimation:** We found that using the mean of points for center estimation was unreliable due to partial viewpoints and noisy outlier points. Simple axis-aligned bounding boxes also led to inaccurate centers. Using an oriented bounding box yielded more reliable coarse center estimates.
*   **Shape Reconstruction:**
    *   The baseline method (NeRF + Marching Cubes from a single image) exhibited missing regions in rear and diagonal views, causing ambiguity in rendering and pose estimation.
    *   Improper axis alignment was observed to cause distortions in X, Y, and Z ratios.
*   **Alignment Steps:**
    *   Using raw object shape estimation without alignment resulted in a complete failure to estimate rotation and translation (near zero performance).
    *   Incorporating coarse size estimation significantly improved the ADD metric.
    *   Incorporating axis alignment further enhanced ADD-S and AR metrics by preventing proportion distortion.
    *   The full method (Coarse Size + Refinement + Axis Alignment) achieved the best results across all metrics and the lowest Chamfer Distance (CD).

Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current approaches to 6D object pose estimation are bifurcated by a significant limitation: the dependency on prior knowledge. Instance-level methods achieve high precision but require exact, textured CAD models of the specific objects during training, rendering them useless for novel objects in the wild. Category-level methods offer some generalization but are restricted to predefined classes and require extensive annotated datasets.

While recent "model-free" approaches attempt to mitigate this by estimating pose from reference images, they suffer from two critical flaws:
1.  **Data Dependency:** Most require multi-view reference images or video sequences (to utilize Structure-from-Motion) to build a sparse point cloud, which is often unavailable in robotic manipulation scenarios.
2.  **Partial Matching Failure:** Methods relying on a single reference image (e.g., via language guidance or feature matching) fail catastrophically when there is little to no visual overlap between the reference (anchor) and the target (query) views, or when significant occlusion occurs. They lack a holistic geometric understanding of the object.

We define the technical problem as the estimation of the relative rigid 6D transformation between a single RGB-D anchor image and a query image for a *novel* object, without access to CAD models, in scenarios characterized by drastic viewpoint changes and occlusions.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose a framework named **Any6D**. Our core hypothesis is that we can bridge the gap between 2D reference images and 3D geometric understanding by leveraging generative Image-to-3D models to hallucinate a "normalized" object shape, and then strictly grounding this shape into the physical world via a **joint object alignment process**.

We hypothesize that existing Image-to-3D models generate shapes that are geometrically consistent but lack metric scale (usually normalized to a unit cube). By treating the **metric scale** and **6D pose** as joint variables in an optimization problem, we can align the hallucinated shape to the single RGB-D anchor image. Once this "proxy" mesh is aligned and scaled to the physical world, it serves as a complete 3D reference, allowing us to estimate the pose of the query image via a render-and-compare strategy. This effectively converts a model-free problem into a model-based one at inference time, enabling robustness even when the anchor and query views are disjoint.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a pipeline that takes an RGB-D anchor image $I_A$ and an RGB-D query image $I_Q$ to estimate the relative pose $\mathbf{T}_{AQ} \in SE(3)$. The transformation $\mathbf{T}_{A \to Q}$ consists of a rotation $R \in SO(3)$ and translation $t \in \mathbb{R}^3$.

### 1. Normalized Shape Reconstruction
First, we will utilize a pre-trained Image-to-3D model (specifically targeting **InstantMesh** for its sparse-view reconstruction capabilities) to process the anchor image $I_A$.
We define the output of this stage as the **normalized object shape** $O_N$.
*   **Constraint:** $O_N$ is generated in a normalized coordinate space (typically $[-1, 1]$ along XYZ axes). It possesses no real-world scale or position.

### 2. Coarse Object Alignment (Initialization)
To utilize $O_N$ for pose estimation, we must transform it into a metric-scale shape $O_M$ by solving for the object size $s \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and the pose $T_{O_M A}$ relative to the anchor.

**Center Estimation:**
Standard centroid calculation is unreliable due to partial visibility in single-view RGB-D. We will implement an **Oriented Bounding Box (OBB)** approach on the segmented point cloud of $I_A$ to estimate the coarse object center, rather than using the mean of points or axis-aligned bounding boxes.

**Axis and Scale Initialization:**
We will perform a search to align the normalized shape $O_N$ with the anchor observation.
1.  We align the OBB with the XYZ axes.
2.  We sample discrete rotation angles.
3.  For each sample, we project the rotated $O_N$ and calculate the Intersection over Union (IoU) with the mask from $I_A$.
4.  The combination of rotation and scale yielding the highest IoU transforms $O_N$ into the initial coarse shape $O_{M'}$.

### 3. Joint Fine Refinement (Pose and Size)
This is the core technical innovation. We will design a refinement module inspired by FoundationPose, but we will modify the hypothesis generation mechanism to solving for **size** simultaneously with pose.

**Sampling Strategy:**
Unlike standard pose refinement which samples only in $SE(3)$, we will sample hypotheses in a joint space $SE(3) \times \mathbb{R}^3$.
We define a size perturbation range $\Delta s \in [s_0, s_1]$. We will empirically set $s_0=0.6$ and $s_1=1.4$.
For each refinement iteration:
1.  Sample pose hypotheses around the current estimate.
2.  Sample size hypotheses within $[s_0, s_1]$ along each axis.
3.  Render the candidate shape $O_{M'}$ using these hypotheses.
4.  Compare the rendering with the query image observation.

**Refinement Cycle:**
The process will alternate between:
1.  **Pose Estimation:** Optimizing $T$ given a fixed $s$.
2.  **Size Estimation:** Optimizing $s$ given a fixed $T$.
3.  **Axis Alignment:** A specific step to correct distortions in X, Y, Z ratios that arise from single-view ambiguity.

**Selection Mechanism:**
We will implement a **Render-and-Compare** selection module.
*   **Pose Ranking Network:** A neural network will encode the cropped observation and the rendered hypothesis into embeddings to quantify alignment quality.
*   **Global Context:** We will apply a self-attention mechanism over the concatenated embeddings of all generated hypotheses to score and select the optimal pose-size pair.

This process yields the final metric-scale object shape $O_M$ and its transform relative to the anchor, $\mathbf{T}_{O_M A}$.

### 4. Relative Pose Estimation
Once the metric-scale shape $O_M$ is established, we treat the query image $I_Q$ as a standard model-based pose estimation task. We utilize the same render-and-compare pipeline to find the transformation from the object to the query, $\mathbf{T}_{O_M Q}$.

The final relative pose $\mathbf{T}_{AQ}$ is computed by composing the two estimated transformations:

$$ \mathbf{T}_{AQ} = (\mathbf{T}_{O_M A})^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{T}_{O_M Q} $$

where $(\mathbf{T}_{O_M A})^{-1}$ transforms from the anchor to the object, and $\mathbf{T}_{O_M Q}$ transforms from the object to the query.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Single-View Metric Recovery:** We expect to demonstrate that generative 3D priors can be strictly grounded in metric space using a single RGB-D image, effectively solving the "scale ambiguity" problem inherent in neural reconstruction.
2.  **Robustness to Disjoint Views:** By reconstructing a complete 3D proxy ($O_M$), we anticipate our method will succeed in estimating poses even when the anchor and query images share **zero visual overlap**, a scenario where feature-matching baselines (like LoFTR or Oryon) theoretically fail.
3.  **Unified Framework:** We will provide a unified architecture that handles object detection, shape hallucination, metric scaling, and 6D pose estimation without requiring CAD models or test-time fine-tuning.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
